notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on mortgage receivers' pre-sale duties.

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage receivers need not pursue planning permission before sale
key_facts: Silven and Chart mortgaged 34 properties to RBS; receivers sold them over 18 months after May 1996.
The appeal concerned six sales where the price was the best reasonably obtainable, but the receivers had abandoned plans to seek planning permission or complete leases before selling.
The receivers had initially investigated planning applications but decided in February 1997 to sell immediately to save costs and achieve quicker repayment for the bank.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission of Chadwick LJ against Patten J's dismissal of mortgagors' claims against receivers, limited to six properties.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; receivers were entitled to sell without delaying to pursue planning permission or grant leases.
enrichment.ratio: Receivers appointed by a mortgagee as agents of the mortgagor owe the same equitable duty on sale as the mortgagee: they must take reasonable care to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable at the date of sale, but they are not obliged to postpone sale or incur expense on improvements such as planning applications or lease completion, and may abandon such steps at any time.
legal_issues: Whether receivers owe a wider duty than mortgagees to take pre-marketing steps to maximise value before exercising the power of sale
Whether commencing planning applications binds receivers not to abandon them before sale
Whether appointment as agent of the mortgagor imposes general agency duties on receivers

notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on IAT fact-finding in blood-feud human rights case.

enrichment.short_title: Albanian blood-feud risk: IAT wrongly overturned adjudicator
key_facts: Mr Koci, an Albanian Muslim, claimed asylum after his father killed two members of a Christian family in a blood feud and was later shot dead; Mr Koci was also shot at in Tirana.
An adjudicator found him credible and held that removal would breach Articles 2 and 3; the asylum claim failed on law after Skenderaj.

The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, preferring the October 2002 CIPU country report to Mr Robertson's expert evidence and treating general improvements in Albania as effective protection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision restoring the Secretary of State's refusal on human rights grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision set aside and adjudicator's human rights determination restored.
enrichment.ratio: The IAT may reverse an adjudicator's findings of fact only if they are plainly wrong or unsustainable; where documentary country evidence does not rationally undermine the adjudicator's acceptance of expert and individual evidence, and the tribunal fails to apply general country findings to the appellant's specific blood-feud history, interference is unlawful.
legal_issues: The standard of review for IAT interference with adjudicator findings of fact
Whether the CIPU report justified rejecting Mr Robertson's expert evidence on blood feuds
Whether failure to seek police protection bars reliance on Article 2 and Article 3
Whether the IAT adequately considered the appellant's individual circumstances

enrichment.short_title: Post Office could not prove exact DSS deficiency after document loss
key_facts: Mrs Mahida, a former sub-postmistress, was sued for £4,341.83 mainly relating to alleged DSS benefit payment discrepancies between 1992 and 1994.
The Post Office had gathered evidence from 1992 but did not issue proceedings until 1997; original dockets, foils and add lists had been destroyed or lost.

At trial the judge relied on secondary schedules compiled by DSS Northern Ireland and Post Office investigators; the defendant had sought but not been given a realistic opportunity to inspect originals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal against county court judgment for the Post Office, with permission on proof of loss and fairness after destruction of documents.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; judgment upheld only for three smaller undisputed items and set aside for the main DSS liability.
enrichment.ratio: Although secondary evidence of accounting discrepancies may be admissible and sufficient to support disciplinary termination, where an institutional creditor loses the primary documents and denies the debtor a fair opportunity to test the schedules, that evidence is not of sufficient weight to prove the precise amount of a debt on the balance of probabilities.
legal_issues: Whether secondary schedule evidence should have been excluded under CPR 31.1(2)
Whether destruction of primary documents rendered the trial unfair under Article 6
Whether October 1994 interview admissions proved the exact debt claimed
Whether the Post Office discharged the burden of proving the precise deficiency

enrichment.short_title: Company distribution on own-share buy-back remains in CGT computation
key_facts: SFOL sold half its CLO shares to a third party and half to CLO itself in 1995 for £871,630 each.
The payment from CLO was a qualifying distribution except for a small capital repayment element.
SFOL contended the distribution element was exempt from corporation tax under ICTA s208 and should be excluded from its chargeable gain; the Revenue assessed it to corporation tax on gains.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Revenue appeal against Etherton J's decision upholding SFOL's appeal from the Special Commissioners.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Special Commissioners' determination restored and assessment upheld.
enrichment.ratio: ICTA section 208 exempts distributions from corporation tax chargeable directly on dividends as income, but does not exclude a distribution forming part of the consideration for a chargeable disposal from the corporation tax capital gains computation; the language 'chargeable on distributions' and the contrast with the second limb of section 208 support treating the payment as consideration for CGT purposes.
legal_issues: Whether ICTA s208 exempts distributions received as consideration for a disposal from corporation tax on chargeable gains
The effect of TCGA s37 where a distribution would be taxable as income to an individual
Whether Hughes v Bank of New Zealand supports a blanket exemption
Whether anomalies in ICTA s13 affect construction of s208

enrichment.short_title: Professional golfer denied appeal on dog-bite career-loss claim
key_facts: Andrew Raitt, a professional golfer, suffered a dog bite to his left little finger in June 1995 shortly after turning professional.
The fingertip was shortened and left numb, but he continued to play well in late 1995 and reached Qualifying School despite the injury.
He claimed the injury adversely affected his grip and long-term earnings, comparing himself to David Howell; liability was already 80% established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral application for permission to appeal against Sir Ian Kennedy's assessment of general and special damages after a four-day trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant bears the burden of proving long-term adverse effect on earning capacity, a judge is entitled to reject subjective evidence unsupported by objective expert observation of the claimant's play before and after the accident, especially where post-accident tournament results and a later road accident complicate causation.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in finding no significant long-term effect on the claimant's golf career
Whether the Scottish road accident affected the judge's findings on the dog bite
Whether loss-of-chance or Smith v Manchester damages were available

enrichment.short_title: Homeless B&B nightly occupancy condition did not breach Article 8
key_facts: Mr Orejudos was accepted as homeless and housed in temporary hotel accommodation under section 193.
Booking agreements required nightly occupancy, daily register signing, and advance notice of absences; repeated unexplained absences led to cancellation.
The authority decided he had become intentionally homeless under section 202; a county court appeal on Article 8 was dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on a point of law from a section 204 county court appeal against an intentionally homeless review decision.
enrichment.ratio: Conditions requiring a homeless person in council-funded bed and breakfast accommodation to sleep there nightly or give a satisfactory reason for absence are an ordinary and necessary incident of temporary daily-charge accommodation and do not interfere with Article 8 private life; Article 8(2) would in any event justify them on cost-control and monitoring grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Cardiff VAT overpayment claim time-barred despite section 33 refund route
key_facts: Cardiff City Council erroneously included non-taxable Grant Agency fees in output tax on VAT returns while also claiming undifferentiated section 33 refunds in box 4.
Because box 4 always exceeded box 3, the Commissioners paid net VAT credits and the council never physically paid tax to HMRC.
PWC claimed over £800,000 in overpaid VAT from 1991 to 2000; HMRC repaid sums within three years but refused earlier periods under section 80(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal in judicial review preliminary issues from Stanley Burnton J's decision on VAT repayment and limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Council appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed; section 33 claim held discharged and early overpayments recoverable only under section 80, which was time-barred.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority includes a section 33 refund claim in box 4 of its VAT return and receives the net box 5 payment, the Commissioners have factually refunded the section 33 claim by set-off; a later attempt to recover historical output-tax overdeclarations is a section 80 repayment claim subject to the three-year limitation, not an outstanding section 33 refund.
legal_issues: Whether Cardiff's claim was a section 33 refund or a section 80 overpayment repayment
Whether section 81(3) set-off discharged the section 33 liability by reference to declared or true VAT liabilities
Whether a repayment trader who never physically pays VAT can use section 80
Whether Regulation 35 imposed a separate limitation period

enrichment.short_title: Phone mast appeal quashed after undisclosed search-area change

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Hutchison sought prior approval for a 12.5m phone mast near Ms Phillips's home in Waterlooville after Havant Borough Council refused approval.
The original application stated a technical search area of about 200m diameter, but Hutchison's appeal statement increased this to about 400m.

The claimant submitted representations before seeing the appeal statement; the inspector accepted Hutchison's alternative-site evidence and allowed the appeal while the mast was erected during litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 challenging an inspector's prior-approval appeal decision; Secretary of State conceded, Hutchison defended.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on procedural unfairness; inspector's decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Alternative sites are a material consideration under PPG8 in telecommunications prior-approval appeals; where an appellant materially changes its stated search area after third parties have made representations and the inspector does not invite further comment, a fair procedure requires re-consultation if the change could have affected alternative-site submissions and may have altered the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether alternative sites were a material consideration where the inspector found no planning harm
Whether Hutchison changed its case on the relevant search area between application and appeal
Whether fairness required further representations after the appeal statement
Whether the claimant was substantially prejudiced

enrichment.short_title: NASS not yet in breach over disabled asylum-seeker children's housing
key_facts: Mrs A and her disabled children claimed asylum and were housed at 50 Clacton Road, Walthamstow; NASS agreed in April 2002 not to disperse them while seeking better local accommodation.
An occupational therapist's May 2002 report said the steep stairs and layout made the property unsuitable for the children's degenerative conditions.
Despite searches by NASS and Waltham Forest, no suitable alternative was found in the area the family insisted on; the family had accepted the property as adequate to remain locally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against Keith J's dismissal of a judicial review claim that NASS failed to provide adequate accommodation under sections 95 and 122.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; NASS not currently in breach, but must continue urgent efforts to secure more suitable accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: Adequacy under section 95 must be assessed by reference to the disabled dependant child's needs, not as if the child were able-bodied; however where a family accepts temporary accommodation in a constrained area knowing better property may be unavailable, and circumstances have not materially changed, NASS is not yet in breach of its section 122 duty though it must keep searching reasonably.
legal_issues: Whether adequate accommodation under section 95/122 takes account of disabled children's needs
Whether local authorities retain section 17 duties while section 122(5) applies
The effect of section 118 on use of local authority housing stock
Whether Article 8 and Article 14 require parity with section 21 National Assistance Act provision
